Mahmud al-Kashgari was a scholar from Kashgar, in today's western China, who wrote the first dictionary of the Turkic languages, the Diwan Lughat al-Turk, "Compendium of the Languages of the Turks".

He probably came from the ruling family of the Kara-Khanids, the first Turkic dynasty to turn Muslim, after Satuq Bughra Khan. He travelled widely among the Turkic peoples and wrote the book in Baghdad in the 1070s, in Arabic, for the Abbasid caliph. At that time the Turkic Seljuks ruled Baghdad, and he wanted Arabs to learn the language of the new masters.

The book explains thousands of Turkic words with proverbs, poems and notes on customs and tribes. It holds a round map of the world centred on Balasagun, with the Turkic lands around it, one of the oldest maps to show Japan.

Only one copy survives, made in 1266. It turned up in Istanbul in the early 1900s. Al-Kashgari was writing in the same Kara-Khanid world, and at the same time, as Yusuf of Balasagun, author of the Kutadgu Bilig.
sum: Mahmud al-Kashgari was a scholar from Kashgar, in today's western China, who wrote the first dictionary of the Turkic languages, the Diwan Lughat al-Turk, "Compendium of the Languages of the Turks".
